summary:
Arauca department stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody rest on court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon, with no one arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Reporting also recalls earlier fatal attacks, including gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá department, flyer campaigns circulated on the street and via WhatsApp announce a "social cleansing" of "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night, and she has been forced to move twice. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's statutory position is frequently cited as among the most advanced in Latin America, yet the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 assessment found a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising. The gap between de jure protection and de facto risk is the central pattern a visitor should carry into Arauca.

The violence documented in the sources is embedded in the country's decades-long civil conflict and in armed-group activity that persists despite the 2016 peace agreement. Killings and threat campaigns are described in reporting as calculated brutality rather than opportunistic crime, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace's July 2023 charges characterise conflict-driven attacks on LGBTI people as gender persecution, a crime against humanity.

Economic marginalisation compounds physical risk. Discrimination is reported to limit trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and in Caquetá trans women are reported to have few options beyond sex work, which narrows the range of neighbourhoods and hours in which a trans visitor or resident can move safely.

Named departments in the sources illustrate a pattern rather than a national average: Guajira for posted kill lists since March 2024, Caquetá for social-cleansing flyers and forced displacement, Antioquia for the Millerey killing. Comparable documentation specific to Arauca does not appear in the inventory.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Arauca-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding appears in the source inventory. The departmental profile rests on the national framework and on documented patterns in other departments, and the presence of armed-group threat campaigns, social-cleansing flyers or trans-specific killings within Arauca itself is not sourced here.

The status of a comprehensive trans law referenced in earlier drafting of this record is unresolved in the current inventory; no source in this pass confirms its passage, content or current stage.

Casualty figures come from different counting bodies and periods and are not directly comparable: 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025, 8 trans women killed between February and April 2024, and 41 killed in 2023 in Guardian reporting against a figure of more than 40 cited elsewhere. Whether any of these victims were in Arauca is not stated.

The inventory does not document whether the notary-based marker change has been applied without obstruction in Arauca, nor whether local registrars there have encountered refusals. It also does not source Arauca-specific access to health care, shelters or police complaint mechanisms for trans visitors.
